title: The Hospital Keeps Its Own Weather II
author: Elena Marquez
poem:
The hallway hums in fluorescent dialect,
a language of machines that refuse metaphor.

My father sleeps beneath a grid of numbers,
each one a fragile agreement with time.

A nurse adjusts the drip
as if calibrating hope.

Outside, the parking lot glints—
ordinary sunlight, indifferent.

Inside, we count breath like currency,
spend it carefully,
wait for interest that never accrues.

Someone laughs down the corridor.
It sounds misplaced,
like summer in a sealed room.

We pretend stability
is not just another word
for delay.

title: Customs Declaration
author: Farah Siddiqui
poem:
At the airport, they ask what I carry.

I want to say: a childhood that no longer translates,
the smell of cardamom pressed into memory,
a grandmother’s voice folded into my tongue.

Instead, I check a box: nothing to declare.

The officer stamps my silence.

Behind me, the line advances—
a procession of edited lives.

I walk forward lighter,
but not free.

Some borders remain
under the skin,
unmarked but permanent.

title: Session Notes
author: Rachel Kim
poem:
You say the word anxiety
as if naming it might shrink it.

I nod,
trace the edge of the couch
like it’s a shoreline.

We circle the same memory,
never landing—
just orbiting impact.

You write something down.
I wonder if it’s me.

At the end, you ask how I feel.

I say: unfinished.

You call that progress.

title: After the Bombing, the Market Reopens
author: Omar Haddad
poem:
Tomatoes arranged in careful pyramids,
as if order could resist memory.

A man sweeps glass into a corner,
small constellations of what shattered.

No one mentions yesterday.

We buy bread.
We ask about prices.
We avoid the crater like a bad habit.

War does not end—
it just learns to whisper.

Even the fruit carries it:
bruised beneath the skin,
still sold as whole.

title: My Mother Teaches Me to Cook Without Recipes
author: Priya Desai
poem:
She never measures.

A pinch means memory.
A handful means trust.

I ask how she knows when it’s right.
She says: you listen.

To what?

To what it reminds you of.

The kitchen fills with something unnamed—
not just spice,
but continuity.

I realize then:
this is how we survive
what history tries to erase.

title: Grief Has No Edges
author: Jonah Stein
poem:
It doesn’t arrive cleanly.

No beginning,
no ending—
just expansion.

I find it in small places:
the empty chair,
the untouched cup.

It refuses containment.

Even joy leaks into it,
changes flavor.

I keep expecting boundaries.

There are none.

title: Fragment / Self
author: Leila Haddad
poem:
I.
A name given
before understanding.

II.
A body negotiating mirrors.

III.
A language that shifts
mid-sentence.

IV.
A question
pretending to be whole.

V.
Still assembling.

title: On the Question of Being
author: Ethan Clarke
poem:
If existence requires witness,
what happens in solitude?

Does the self persist
without reflection,
or does it dissolve
into possibility?

I sit in a room
with no mirrors,
no language,
no one to confirm.

Still,
something remains.

But I cannot prove it.

title: The Forest Teaches Subtraction
author: Hannah Wu
poem:
Leaves fall without ceremony.

The tree does not mourn them.

It understands
what must be released
for survival.

I walk beneath this lesson,
carrying too much.

Even the ground
knows how to let go.

I am still learning.

title: Passport Photo
author: Miguel Alvarez
poem:
Neutral expression.
No smiling.
No history visible.

I sit under fluorescent judgment,
compressing identity
into two inches.

They want clarity.
They get approximation.

This face has crossed too much
to be simplified.

Still,
the camera insists.

title: Code Blue, Room 417
author: Daniel Cho
poem:
The announcement fractures the hallway—
code blue, as if language could soften urgency.

Shoes strike tile in practiced panic.
A curtain snaps closed.

Inside, the body becomes negotiation:
hands pressing time back into a chest,
a machine insisting on rhythm.

Outside, we pretend not to listen.
We study our phones,
the scuffed floor,
anything but mortality rehearsing nearby.

When it ends—
whatever ending means—
the hallway resumes.

But something lingers,
like a question
no one is trained to answer.

title: My Name Mispronounced at Roll Call
author: Sana Rahman
poem:
Each syllable bent,
as if my name were negotiable.

I raise my hand anyway.
Present.

The classroom learns me incorrectly.
I allow it—
a small surrender repeated daily.

Later, at home,
my mother says it whole,
like a prayer restored.

I realize then:
identity fractures quietly,
not in violence,
but in permission.

title: Instructions for Breathing During Panic
author: Lucas Bennett
poem:
Step 1: Notice the air.

Step 2: Convince your body
it is not drowning.

Step 3: Fail.

The chest tightens
like a locked room.

You count—
not numbers,
but exits.

The therapist says:
you are safe.

Your body disagrees.

Eventually,
the wave recedes
without apology.

title: Ceasefire
author: Omar Haddad
poem:
They call it ceasefire
as if silence were peace.

The buildings remain broken,
the windows still remembering impact.

Children return to the street
with cautious laughter,
testing the air.

Nothing has ended.

It has only paused—
violence holding its breath,
waiting for permission to resume.

title: My Grandmother’s Hands
author: Ana Rodriguez
poem:
They move without hesitation,
remembering what the mind forgets.

Dough folds into itself,
patient as tradition.

She does not measure.
She knows.

I try to imitate,
but my hands lack history.

Some knowledge
cannot be written—
only inherited.

title: After the Funeral
author: Jonah Stein
poem:
We return to ordinary tasks—
washing dishes,
answering messages.

Grief waits politely
in the background.

It does not interrupt.

Later, alone,
it expands to fill the room.

I realize then:
loss is not an event.

It is a condition.

title: Experiment: Identity Without Language
author: Leila Haddad
poem:
[Remove all names]
[Remove all categories]

What remains?

A body
moving through space.

A set of reactions.

A pulse.

Conclusion:
identity persists
but becomes unrecognizable.

title: On Being Observed
author: Ethan Clarke
poem:
If a self exists alone,
is it complete?

Or does it require
another’s gaze
to stabilize?

I perform myself
in reflections—
mirrors,
windows,
eyes.

Without them,
I flicker.

title: The Ocean Refuses Containment
author: Hannah Wu
poem:
You draw a line on a map
and call it shore.

The ocean disagrees.

It moves,
erases,
returns.

I stand at the edge,
watching boundaries fail.

Some things
cannot be held
in definition.

title: Visa Expiration Date
author: Miguel Alvarez
poem:
My life reduced
to a printed deadline.

I exist legally
until I do not.

Time becomes external,
measured in permissions.

I check the date
more often than my reflection.

Identity,
temporary.

title: Radiology Waiting Room
author: Marta Velasquez
poem:
We sit in borrowed stillness,
holding forms like fragile agreements.

The television murmurs weather forecasts
no one believes in.

Inside the machine,
someone becomes image—
reduced to shadows,
contrasts,
interpretation.

A technician calls a name.
Another body enters uncertainty.

We avoid each other’s eyes,
as if diagnosis were contagious.

Time here does not pass.
It accumulates.

title: Accent
author: Julian Park
poem:
They say I have one
as if it were optional.

I try to smooth the edges,
file down the sound of origin.

Still, certain words betray me—
vowels shaped by elsewhere.

At home,
I let the language return whole,
full-bodied,
unapologetic.

Between these two versions,
I exist
partially translated.

title: The Body During Insomnia
author: Claire Donovan
poem:
Night stretches beyond intention.

The clock insists on movement,
but the body refuses rest.

Thought loops—
an argument without resolution.

Even silence becomes loud.

I catalog each breath,
each shift,
each failure to surrender.

Morning will arrive anyway.

It always does,
indifferent to readiness.

title: Aftermath, Domestic
author: Rami Khalil
poem:
The war leaves quietly.

A plate still chipped.
A wall slightly uneven.

We repair what we can name.

But the air—

The air remembers everything.

It thickens in certain rooms,
pauses at thresholds.

We open windows
that do not clear it.

Some damage
refuses visibility.

title: Recipe for Remembering
author: Amara Singh
poem:
Begin with something inherited.

Add heat—
not too much,
just enough to release what was hidden.

Stir continuously.
Do not leave unattended.

When it begins to change,
do not panic.

This is how memory works:
transforming without asking.

Serve while still recognizable.

title: The Day After Loss
author: Evan Pierce
poem:
Nothing marks it.

The same light enters the room.
The same sounds persist.

Only the absence shifts—
more defined,
more present.

I reach for what is no longer there
out of habit.

The body learns slowly.

Grief does not announce itself.

It integrates.

title: Fragmented Thesis on Selfhood
author: Noah Fischer
poem:
1. The self is unstable.

2. Observation alters identity.

3. Memory is unreliable data.

4. Language introduces distortion.

5. Conclusion:
   no conclusion possible.

Appendix:
   still, we proceed
   as if coherence exists.

title: Mirror Without Reflection
author: Isabel Romero
poem:
Imagine a mirror
that refuses you.

Glass intact,
light functioning,
but no image returned.

Would you still exist
in certainty?

Or would identity
require proof?

title: Tide Pools
author: Hannah Wu
poem:
Small worlds left behind
by something larger.

The ocean withdraws,
but not completely.

Life remains
in pockets,
adapting.

I study these fragments,
recognize the pattern:

we survive
in what is left.

title: Checkpoint
author: Omar Haddad
poem:
Stop.

Wait.

Explain yourself.

The questions are always the same,
only the answers change.

I present documents.
They present doubt.

Between us,
an invisible line
holds all the power.

I cross eventually.

But not unchanged.

title: Oncology Ward, 6 A.M.
author: Marisol Vega
poem:
Morning arrives without permission.

A cart rattles past—
pills sorted into small inevitabilities.

The woman across the hall
counts her breaths aloud,
as if naming them keeps them present.

I watch sunlight
hesitate at the window,
unwilling to enter this negotiation.

We all wait for results
that will redefine us.

Even hope
feels clinical here.

title: Dual Citizenship
author: Adil Khan
poem:
Two passports.
Two versions of belonging.

In one place,
I am from somewhere else.

In the other,
I have already left.

Customs asks where I live.

I hesitate—
choose an answer
that feels least incorrect.

Home becomes
an administrative decision.

title: The Therapist Mentions Patterns
author: Eliza Grant
poem:
You say it like a discovery—
as if repetition were accidental.

I nod,
recognizing the shape of it:

same fear,
different context.

We map my history
like a recurring storm.

You ask what breaks the cycle.

I say:
I don't know where it begins.

title: The Sound After Shelling
author: Rami Khalil
poem:
Not silence—

something heavier.

Air thick with what just happened.

A dog barks
then stops,
as if remembering.

We listen
for what might follow.

Nothing comes.

That is the most frightening part.

title: Spice Drawer Inventory
author: Priya Desai
poem:
Turmeric—
stains everything it touches.

Cumin—
earth held in powder.

Cardamom—
something almost sweet.

Each jar
labeled in my mother’s handwriting.

I open them carefully,
release small histories.

Cooking becomes
an act of remembering
what cannot be written down.

title: Condolences
author: Jonah Stein
poem:
People say I’m sorry
like it completes a sentence.

I nod,
accept the offering.

What else is there?

Language fails
at the scale of absence.

Still,
we repeat it—
ritual over meaning.

title: Notes Toward a Definition of Self
author: Ethan Clarke
poem:
The self is:

not fixed

not singular

not fully knowable

The self is also:

persistent

contradictory

unfinished

Conclusion:
working draft.

title: The River in Winter
author: Hannah Wu
poem:
Surface frozen.

Movement continues below.

From above,
stillness.

From within,
current.

I think of the ways
we appear unchanged
while everything shifts
out of sight.

title: Philosophy Lecture, Half-Empty Room
author: Noah Fischer
poem:
The professor asks
what it means to exist.

A student checks their phone.

Another stares at the desk
as if the answer might appear there.

I consider raising my hand,
but the question feels larger
than speech.

The bell rings.

We leave
without resolution.

title: Name Change Form
author: Miguel Alvarez
poem:
Print clearly.

Use black ink.

Do not erase.

I write a version of myself
that fits the space provided.

The old name lingers
in muscle memory.

The new one
feels provisional.

Identity,
submitted for approval.

title: ICU Night Log
author: Samuel Ortega
poem:
02:13 — machine alarm
02:14 — nurse enters
02:16 — adjustment made

Time recorded in fragments.

No one writes:
fear present,
hope unstable.

The chart remains clinical.

The body does not.

title: Language Barrier
author: Mei Lin Zhou
poem:
We stand across from each other
with words that refuse passage.

I gesture.
You repeat.

Meaning hovers between us,
unclaimed.

We both nod—
approximation accepted.

Understanding,
incomplete but functional.

title: Medication Side Effects
author: Claire Donovan
poem:
Drowsiness.
Dizziness.
Dry mouth.

The list continues,
longer than relief.

I take it anyway.

Some cures
require negotiation.

I trade clarity
for quiet.

title: After the Siren Stops
author: Rami Khalil
poem:
Silence returns
like nothing happened.

But we remain alert,
bodies unwilling to trust it.

The absence of sound
is not peace.

It is waiting.

title: Family Table, Missing Chair
author: Ana Rodriguez
poem:
We set the table anyway.

Habit outweighs accuracy.

A space remains—
not acknowledged,
but present.

We pass dishes,
avoid looking directly at it.

Absence takes a seat
without invitation.

title: The Problem of Continuity
author: Ethan Clarke
poem:
If the self changes constantly,
what remains the same?

Memory?
Unreliable.

Body?
Temporary.

Name?
Assigned.

Still,
we insist on identity
as if it were stable.

title: Forest Floor
author: Hannah Wu
poem:
Decay feeds growth.

What falls
returns differently.

Nothing wasted,
only transformed.

I walk carefully,
aware that every step
is part of the cycle.

title: Immigration Form Question 12
author: Miguel Alvarez
poem:
Have you ever—

The question begins
before I finish reading.

My history reduced
to checkboxes.

Yes.
No.

Neither answer
feels sufficient.

title: Therapy Exit
author: Rachel Kim
poem:
The session ends
mid-thought.

I carry the unfinished sentence
out into the street.

Cars pass.
People move.

Nothing reflects
what just shifted.

Change happens quietly.

title: Identity, Temporary Housing
author: Leila Haddad
poem:
I live inside definitions
that expire.

Each label
comes with conditions.

I renew when necessary,
adjust when required.

The self remains
on short-term lease.
